The rest is convenience or for advanced testing.\n\n## 2.1) How profiles interact with Sensei-check rules\n\nSensei-check uses the conversations generated by Sensei Profiles to run **metamorphic rules**. In that pipeline:\n\n- Profiles generate conversations and define what should be extracted in `chatbot.output`.\n- Sensei-check rules then read those extracted outputs via expressions like `conv[i].field_name`.\n\n### 2.1.1 `chatbot.output` as the contract for rules\n\nThe `chatbot.output` section defines a **schema** of fields that:\n\n- the extractor will populate at the end of each conversation, and\n- Sensei-check rules will refer to as `conv[i].<field_name>`.\n\nExample:\n\n```yaml\nchatbot:\n  output:\n    - total_price:\n        type: currency\n        description: \"Final price including taxes and add-ons\"\n    - booking_id:\n        type: string\n        description: \"Booking reference\"\n```\n\nIn rules, you might then write:\n\n```yaml\nwhen: conv[0].booking_id is not None\nthen: extract_float(conv[0].total_price) > 0\n```\n\nHere, `total_price` and `booking_id` come directly from `chatbot.output`.\n\n### 2.1.2 Designing `chatbot.output` with rules in mind\n\nWhen you design a profile, think about:\n\n- Which **business properties** or **behavioural invariants** you want to test with rules later (e.g., monotonicity of price, field completeness, uniqueness, topic scope).\n- Which fields the rules will need to access.\n\nBest practices:\n\n- Use stable, descriptive names (e.g., `total_price`, `opening_hours`, `order_id`) instead of names tied to one particular experiment.\n- Avoid duplicating the same concept under many different names across profiles; \"content\": \"# Sensei Profiles: How It Works and How to Author a Profile\\n\\n> This guide focuses on **profiles**—the YAML files that define how Sensei’s user simulator behaves—and provides just enough context about how Sensei runs so you can create, validate, and execute profiles confidently.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1) What Sensei Is (in one minute)\\n\\nSensei is a **user simulator** for chatbot testing. You give it a profile (a YAML file) that describes the simulated user’s language, role, context, goals, data types, interaction style, and so on. Sensei then talks to your target chatbot, logs the conversation, and can extract structured outputs for validation.\\n\\n- **Profiles are YAML** and live under a project’s `profiles/` directory.\\n- **Custom data types** go in `types/`.\\n- **Optional personalities** (prompt fragments) go in `personalities/`.\\n- You can execute Sensei by passing CLI arguments **or** by using a `run.yml` inside your project.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2) Project Layout (where profiles live)\\n\\nWhen you run the project initializer, Sensei creates a folder with these key locations:\\n\\n```\\nproject_folder/\\n  personalities/     # optional prompt snippets for user “personas”\\n  profiles/          # your user profile YAMLs (or a folder of profiles)\\n  rules/             # rules and metamorpfic rules for testing\\n  types/             # custom data-type YAMLs (regex + extraction schema)\\n  run.yml            # optional: run configuration so you don’t type long CLIs\\n```\\n\\nOnly `profiles/` (and optionally `types/` and `personalities/`) matter for authoring profiles. The rest is convenience or for advanced testing.\\n\\n## 2.1) How profiles interact with Sensei-check rules\\n\\nSensei-check uses the conversations generated by Sensei Profiles to run **metamorphic rules**. In that pipeline:\\n\\n- Profiles generate conversations and define what should be extracted in `chatbot.output`.\\n- Sensei-check rules then read those extracted outputs via expressions like `conv[i].field_name`.\\n\\n### 2.1.1 `chatbot.output` as the contract for rules\\n\\nThe `chatbot.output` section defines a **schema** of fields that:\\n\\n- the extractor will populate at the end of each conversation, and\\n- Sensei-check rules will refer to as `conv[i].<field_name>`.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n```yaml\\nchatbot:\\n  output:\\n    - total_price:\\n        type: currency\\n        description: \\\"Final price including taxes and add-ons\\\"\\n    - booking_id:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"Booking reference\\\"\\n```\\n\\nIn rules, you might then write:\\n\\n```yaml\\nwhen: conv[0].booking_id is not None\\nthen: extract_float(conv[0].total_price) > 0\\n```\\n\\nHere, `total_price` and `booking_id` come directly from `chatbot.output`.\\n\\n### 2.1.2 Designing `chatbot.output` with rules in mind\\n\\nWhen you design a profile, think about:\\n\\n- Which **business properties** or **behavioural invariants** you want to test with rules later (e.g., monotonicity of price, field completeness, uniqueness, topic scope).\\n- Which fields the rules will need to access.\\n\\nBest practices:\\n\\n- Use stable, descriptive names (e.g., `total_price`, `opening_hours`, `order_id`) instead of names tied to one particular experiment.\\n- Avoid duplicating the same concept under many different names across profiles; reuse names when semantics are the same.\\n- If you know you will write rules about a field, make sure it appears in `chatbot.output` and has the right `type` (e.g., `currency` instead of a raw `string`).\\n\\n### 2.1.3 Profile-bound vs global rules\\n\\nFrom the profile’s viewpoint, you will typically see two kinds of rules:\\n\\n1. **Profile-bound rules**\\n\\n   - Target a specific profile (e.g., `pizza_order_summary`).\\n   - Rely on its `chatbot.output` fields (e.g., `size`, `toppings`, `price`).\\n   - The rule should be updated if you rename or remove these fields.\\n\\n2. **Global rules**\\n\\n   - Apply to many profiles or the whole dataset.\\n   - Use generic helpers such as `only_talks_about`, `language`, `responds_in_same_language`, `repeated_answers`, `data_collected`, etc.\\n   - Do not require a particular `chatbot.output` schema to make sense.\\n\\nWhen you create or change a profile, ask:\\n\\n- “Which profile-bound rules might be affected if I rename/remove this field?”\\n- “Do I need to add a new field so that rules can express the checks I care about?”\\n\\nKeeping this contract in mind will make your rules and profiles evolve together without surprises.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3) Profile File: high‑level anatomy\\n\\nA profile is a single YAML file (or a **folder** with multiple YAMLs for batch execution). These are the top-level sections you’ll use most:\\n\\n```yaml\\ntest_name: \\\"string\\\"\\n\\nllm:\\n  temperature: float\\n  model: \\\"provider-specific name\\\"\\n  model_prov: \\\"langchain provider key\\\"\\n  format:\\n    type: text | speech\\n    # config: path/to/speech_config.yml   # (only for type: speech)\\n\\nuser:\\n  language: English | Spanish | ...\\n  role: \\\"prompt describing the simulated user\\\"\\n  context:\\n    - personality: personalities/<file>.yml   # optional\\n    - \\\"freeform constraints, facts, preferences …\\\"\\n  goals:\\n    - \\\"freeform goal with {{variables}}\\\"\\n    - variable_name:\\n        function: default|random|forward|another|pairwise(...)\\n        type: string|int|float|<custom>\\n        data: ... # list, range, generator, or LLM-generated list\\n\\nchatbot:\\n  is_starter: true|false\\n  fallback: \\\"bot’s real fallback message\\\"\\n  output:\\n    - field_name:\\n        type: <primitive|list[primitive]|custom>\\n        description: \\\"what to extract at the end\\\"\\n\\nconversation:\\n  number: <int> | combinations | combinations(0.6) | combinations(0.6, pairwise)\\n  max_cost: <float $>      # optional: cap spend for the whole run\\n  goal_style:              # how/when a conversation ends\\n    steps: <int> | random steps: <max> | all_answered:\\n      export: true|false   # export the verification dataframe\\n      limit: <int>         # safety stop; default 30 if omitted\\n    max_cost: <float $>    # optional: per‑conversation cost cap\\n  interaction_style: # choose one or many from here\\n    - long phrases | change your mind | change language: [italian, portuguese, ...] | make spelling mistakes | single questions | all questions\\n    - random: [any of the above] # there can be some interaction styles fixed and then some random, check the docs of the interaction_style section\\n```\\n\\n> Tip: Each **goal** can be a plain string 4.1 Variables in text\\n\\nWrite prompts like:\\n`- \\\"Order a {{size}} pizza with {{toppings}} and {{cans}} cans of {{drink}}\\\"`\\n\\nEach `{{variable}}` must be declared elsewhere in the `goals` list_functions/number_list.py\\n    function_name: shuffle_list      # or your custom function\\n    args: [1, 6, 2]    # can be completed with a yaml containing a list (args: \"content\": \"# Sensei Profiles: How It Works and How to Author a Profile\\n\\n> This guide focuses on **profiles**—the YAML files that define how Sensei’s user simulator behaves—and provides just enough context about how Sensei runs so you can create, validate, and execute profiles confidently.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1) What Sensei Is (in one minute)\\n\\nSensei is a **user simulator** for chatbot testing. You give it a profile (a YAML file) that describes the simulated user’s language, role, context, goals, data types, interaction style, and so on. Sensei then talks to your target chatbot, logs the conversation, and can extract structured outputs for validation.\\n\\n- **Profiles are YAML** and live under a project’s `profiles/` directory.\\n- **Custom data types** go in `types/`.\\n- **Optional personalities** (prompt fragments) go in `personalities/`.\\n- You can execute Sensei by passing CLI arguments **or** by using a `run.yml` inside your project.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2) Project Layout (where profiles live)\\n\\nWhen you run the project initializer, Sensei creates a folder with these key locations:\\n\\n```\\nproject_folder/\\n  personalities/     # optional prompt snippets for user “personas”\\n  profiles/          # your user profile YAMLs (or a folder of profiles)\\n  rules/             # rules and metamorpfic rules for testing\\n  types/             # custom data-type YAMLs (regex + extraction schema)\\n  run.yml            # optional: run configuration so you don’t type long CLIs\\n```\\n\\nOnly `profiles/` (and optionally `types/` and `personalities/`) matter for authoring profiles. The rest is convenience or for advanced testing.\\n\\n## 2.1) How profiles interact with Sensei-check rules\\n\\nSensei-check uses the conversations generated by Sensei Profiles to run **metamorphic rules**. In that pipeline:\\n\\n- Profiles generate conversations and define what should be extracted in `chatbot.output`.\\n- Sensei-check rules then read those extracted outputs via expressions like `conv[i].field_name`.\\n\\n### 2.1.1 `chatbot.output` as the contract for rules\\n\\nThe `chatbot.output` section defines a **schema** of fields that:\\n\\n- the extractor will populate at the end of each conversation, and\\n- Sensei-check rules will refer to as `conv[i].<field_name>`.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n```yaml\\nchatbot:\\n  output:\\n    - total_price:\\n        type: currency\\n        description: \\\"Final price including taxes and add-ons\\\"\\n    - booking_id:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"Booking reference\\\"\\n```\\n\\nIn rules, you might then write:\\n\\n```yaml\\nwhen: conv[0].booking_id is not None\\nthen: extract_float(conv[0].total_price) > 0\\n```\\n\\nHere, `total_price` and `booking_id` come directly from `chatbot.output`.\\n\\n### 2.1.2 Designing `chatbot.output` with rules in mind\\n\\nWhen you design a profile, think about:\\n\\n- Which **business properties** or **behavioural invariants** you want to test with rules later (e.g., monotonicity of price, field completeness, uniqueness, topic scope).\\n- Which fields the rules will need to access.\\n\\nBest practices:\\n\\n- Use stable, descriptive names (e.g., `total_price`, `opening_hours`, `order_id`) instead of names tied to one particular experiment.\\n- Avoid duplicating the same concept under many different names across profiles; reuse names when semantics are the same.\\n- If you know you will write rules about a field, make sure it appears in `chatbot.output` and has the right `type` (e.g., `currency` instead of a raw `string`).\\n\\n### 2.1.3 Profile-bound vs global rules\\n\\nFrom the profile’s viewpoint, you will typically see two kinds of rules:\\n\\n1. **Profile-bound rules**\\n\\n   - Target a specific profile (e.g., `pizza_order_summary`).\\n   - Rely on its `chatbot.output` fields (e.g., `size`, `toppings`, `price`).\\n   - The rule should be updated if you rename or remove these fields.\\n\\n2. **Global rules**\\n\\n   - Apply to many profiles or the whole dataset.\\n   - Use generic helpers such as `only_talks_about`, `language`, `responds_in_same_language`, `repeated_answers`, `data_collected`, etc.\\n   - Do not require a particular `chatbot.output` schema to make sense.\\n\\nWhen you create or change a profile, ask:\\n\\n- “Which profile-bound rules might be affected if I rename/remove this field?”\\n- “Do I need to add a new field so that rules can express the checks I care about?”\\n\\nKeeping this contract in mind will make your rules and profiles evolve together without surprises.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3) Profile File: high‑level anatomy\\n\\nA profile is a single YAML file (or a **folder** with multiple YAMLs for batch execution). These are the top-level sections you’ll use most:\\n\\n```yaml\\ntest_name: \\\"string\\\"\\n\\nllm:\\n  temperature: float\\n  model: \\\"provider-specific name\\\"\\n  model_prov: \\\"langchain provider key\\\"\\n  format:\\n    type: text | speech\\n    # config: path/to/speech_config.yml   # (only for type: speech)\\n\\nuser:\\n  language: English | Spanish | ...\\n  role: \\\"prompt describing the simulated user\\\"\\n  context:\\n    - personality: personalities/<file>.yml   # optional\\n    - \\\"freeform constraints, facts, preferences …\\\"\\n  goals:\\n    - \\\"freeform goal with {{variables}}\\\"\\n    - variable_name:\\n        function: default|random|forward|another|pairwise(...)\\n        type: string|int|float|<custom>\\n        data: ... # list, range, max_cost: <float $>      # optional: cap spend for the whole run\\n  goal_style:              # how/when a conversation ends\\n    steps: <int> | random steps: <max> | all_answered:\\n      export: interaction_style: # choose one or many from here\\n    - long phrases | change your mind | change language: [italian, portuguese, ...] | make spelling mistakes | single questions | all questions\\n 4.1 Variables in text\\n\\nWrite prompts like:\\n`- \\\"Order a {{size}} pizza with {{toppings}} and {{cans}} cans of {{drink}}\\\"`\\n\\nEach `{{variable}}` must be declared elsewhere in the `goals` `.\\n\\n\\n**Examples**\\n\\n`types/phone_number.yml`:\\n\\n```yaml\\nname: phone_number\\ntype_description: A phone number\\nformat: r\\\"^\\\\d{3}-\\\\d{7}$\\\"\\nextraction: list_functions/number_list.py\\n    function_name: shuffle_list      # or your custom function\\n    args: [1, 6, 2]    # can be completed with a yaml containing a list (args: list_functions/list_of_things.yml)\\n  ```\\n\\n### 4.4 Fill functions (how values are chosen each run)\\n\\n- `default()` → use **all** items.\\n- `random()` → pick **one** at random.\\n- `random(5)` You give it a profile (a YAML file) that describes the simulated user’s language, role, context, goals, data types, interaction style, and so on. Sensei then talks to your target chatbot, logs the conversation, and can extract structured outputs for validation.\\n\\n- **Profiles are YAML** and live under a project’s `profiles/` directory.\\n- **Custom data types** go in `types/`.\\n- **Optional personalities** (prompt fragments) go in `personalities/`.\\n- You can execute Sensei by passing CLI arguments **or** by using a `run.yml` inside your project.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2) Project Layout (where profiles live)\\n\\nWhen you run the project initializer, Sensei creates a folder with these key locations:\\n\\n```\\nproject_folder/\\n  personalities/     # optional prompt snippets for user “personas”\\n  profiles/          # your user profile YAMLs (or a folder of profiles)\\n  rules/             # rules and metamorpfic rules for testing\\n  types/             # custom data-type YAMLs (regex + extraction schema)\\n  run.yml            # optional: run configuration so you don’t type long CLIs\\n```\\n\\nOnly `profiles/` (and optionally `types/` and `personalities/`) matter for authoring profiles. The rest is convenience or for advanced testing.\\n\\n## 2.1) How profiles interact with Sensei-check rules\\n\\nSensei-check uses the conversations generated by Sensei Profiles to run **metamorphic rules**. In that pipeline:\\n\\n- Profiles generate conversations and define what should be extracted in `chatbot.output`.\\n- Sensei-check rules then read those extracted outputs via expressions like `conv[i].field_name`.\\n\\n### 2.1.1 `chatbot.output` as the contract for rules\\n\\nThe `chatbot.output` section defines a **schema** of fields that:\\n\\n- the extractor will populate at the end of each conversation, and\\n- Sensei-check rules will refer to as `conv[i].<field_name>`.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n```yaml\\nchatbot:\\n  output:\\n    - total_price:\\n        type: currency\\n        description: \\\"Final price including taxes and add-ons\\\"\\n    - booking_id:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"Booking reference\\\"\\n```\\n\\nIn rules, you might then write:\\n\\n```yaml\\nwhen: conv[0].booking_id is not None\\nthen: extract_float(conv[0].total_price) > 0\\n```\\n\\nHere, `total_price` and `booking_id` come directly from `chatbot.output`.\\n\\n### 2.1.2 Designing `chatbot.output` with rules in mind\\n\\nWhen you design a profile, think about:\\n\\n- Which **business properties** or **behavioural invariants** you want to test with rules later (e.g., monotonicity of price, field completeness, uniqueness, topic scope).\\n- Which fields the rules will need to access.\\n\\nBest practices:\\n\\n- Use stable, descriptive names (e.g., `total_price`, `opening_hours`, `order_id`) instead of names tied to one particular experiment.\\n- Avoid duplicating the same concept under many different names across profiles; reuse names when semantics are the same.\\n- If you know you will write rules about a field, make sure it appears in `chatbot.output` and has the right `type` (e.g., `currency` instead of a raw `string`).\\n\\n### 2.1.3 Profile-bound vs global rules\\n\\nFrom the profile’s viewpoint, you will typically see two kinds of rules:\\n\\n1. **Profile-bound rules**\\n\\n   - Target a specific profile (e.g., `pizza_order_summary`).\\n   - Rely on its `chatbot.output` fields (e.g., `size`, `toppings`, `price`).\\n   - The rule should be updated if you rename or remove these fields.\\n\\n2. **Global rules**\\n\\n   - Apply to many profiles or the whole dataset.\\n   - Use generic helpers such as `only_talks_about`, `language`, `responds_in_same_language`, `repeated_answers`, `data_collected`, etc.\\n   - Do not require a particular `chatbot.output` schema to make sense.\\n\\nWhen you create or change a profile, ask:\\n\\n- “Which profile-bound rules might be affected if I rename/remove this field?”\\n- “Do I need to add a new field so that rules can express the checks I care about?”\\n\\nKeeping this contract in mind will make your rules and profiles evolve together without surprises.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3) Profile File: high‑level anatomy\\n\\nA profile is a single YAML file (or a **folder** with multiple YAMLs for batch execution). These are the top-level sections you’ll use most:\\n\\n```yaml\\ntest_name: \\\"string\\\"\\n\\nllm:\\n  temperature: float\\n  model: \\\"provider-specific name\\\"\\n  model_prov: \\\"langchain provider key\\\"\\n  format:\\n    type: text | speech\\n    # config: path/to/speech_config.yml   # (only for type: speech)\\n\\nuser:\\n  language: English | Spanish | ...\\n  role: \\\"prompt <primitive|list[primitive]|custom>\\n        description: \\\"what to extract at the end\\\"\\n\\nconversation:\\n  number: <int> | combinations | combinations(0.6) | combinations(0.6, pairwise)\\n testing. You give it a profile (a YAML file) that describes the simulated user’s language, role, context, goals, data types, interaction style, and so on. Sensei then talks to your target chatbot, logs the conversation, and can extract structured outputs for validation.\\n\\n- **Profiles are YAML** and live under a project’s `profiles/` directory.\\n- **Custom data types** go in `types/`.\\n- **Optional personalities** (prompt fragments) go in `personalities/`.\\n- You can execute Sensei by passing CLI arguments **or** by using a `run.yml` inside your project.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2) Project Layout (where profiles live)\\n\\nWhen you run the project initializer, Sensei creates a folder with these key locations:\\n\\n```\\nproject_folder/\\n  personalities/     # optional prompt snippets for user “personas”\\n  profiles/          # your user profile YAMLs (or a folder of profiles)\\n  rules/             # rules and metamorpfic rules for testing\\n  types/             # custom data-type YAMLs (regex + extraction schema)\\n  run.yml            # optional: run configuration so you don’t type long CLIs\\n```\\n\\nOnly `profiles/` (and optionally `types/` and `personalities/`) matter for authoring profiles. The rest is convenience or for advanced testing.\\n\\n## 2.1) How profiles interact with Sensei-check rules\\n\\nSensei-check uses the conversations generated by Sensei Profiles to run **metamorphic rules**. In that pipeline:\\n\\n- Profiles generate conversations and define what should be extracted in `chatbot.output`.\\n- Sensei-check rules then read those extracted outputs via expressions like `conv[i].field_name`.\\n\\n### 2.1.1 `chatbot.output` as the contract for rules\\n\\nThe `chatbot.output` section defines a **schema** of fields that:\\n\\n- the extractor will populate at the end of each conversation, and\\n- Sensei-check rules will refer to as `conv[i].<field_name>`.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n```yaml\\nchatbot:\\n  output:\\n    - total_price:\\n        type: currency\\n        description: \\\"Final price including taxes and add-ons\\\"\\n    - booking_id:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"Booking reference\\\"\\n```\\n\\nIn rules, you might then write:\\n\\n```yaml\\nwhen: conv[0].booking_id is not None\\nthen: extract_float(conv[0].total_price) > 0\\n```\\n\\nHere, `total_price` and `booking_id` come directly from `chatbot.output`.\\n\\n### 2.1.2 Designing `chatbot.output` with rules in mind\\n\\nWhen you design a profile, think about:\\n\\n- Which **business properties** or **behavioural invariants** you want to test with rules later (e.g., monotonicity of price, field completeness, uniqueness, topic scope).\\n- Which fields the rules will need to access.\\n\\nBest practices:\\n\\n- Use stable, descriptive names (e.g., `total_price`, `opening_hours`, `order_id`) instead of names tied to one particular experiment.\\n- Avoid duplicating the same concept under many different names across profiles; interaction_style: # choose one or many from here\\n    - long phrases | change your mind | change language: [italian, portuguese, ...] | make spelling mistakes | single questions | all questions\\n \"content\": \"# Sensei Profiles: How It Works and How to Author a Profile\\n\\n> This guide focuses on **profiles**—the YAML files that define how Sensei’s user simulator behaves—and provides just enough context about how Sensei runs so you can create, validate, and execute profiles confidently.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1) What Sensei Is (in one minute)\\n\\nSensei is a **user simulator** for chatbot testing. You give it a profile (a YAML file) that describes the simulated user’s language, role, context, goals, data types, interaction style, and so on. Sensei then talks to your target chatbot, logs the conversation, and can extract structured outputs for validation.\\n\\n- **Profiles are YAML** and live under a project’s `profiles/` directory.\\n- **Custom data types** go in `types/`.\\n- **Optional personalities** (prompt fragments) go in `personalities/`.\\n- You can execute Sensei by passing CLI arguments **or** by using a `run.yml` inside your project.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2) Project Layout (where profiles live)\\n\\nWhen you run the project initializer, Sensei creates a folder with these key locations:\\n\\n```\\nproject_folder/\\n  personalities/     # optional prompt snippets for user “personas”\\n  profiles/          # your user profile YAMLs (or a folder of profiles)\\n  rules/             # rules and metamorpfic rules for testing\\n  types/             # custom data-type YAMLs (regex + extraction schema)\\n  run.yml            # optional: run configuration so you don’t type long CLIs\\n```\\n\\nOnly `profiles/` (and optionally `types/` and `personalities/`) matter for authoring profiles. The rest is convenience or for advanced testing.\\n\\n## 2.1) How profiles interact with Sensei-check rules\\n\\nSensei-check uses the conversations generated by Sensei Profiles to run **metamorphic rules**. In that pipeline:\\n\\n- Profiles generate conversations and define what should be extracted in `chatbot.output`.\\n- Sensei-check rules then read those extracted outputs via expressions like `conv[i].field_name`.\\n\\n### 2.1.1 `chatbot.output` as the contract for rules\\n\\nThe `chatbot.output` section defines a **schema** of fields that:\\n\\n- the extractor will populate at the end of each conversation, and\\n- Sensei-check rules will refer to as `conv[i].<field_name>`.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n```yaml\\nchatbot:\\n  output:\\n    - total_price:\\n        type: currency\\n        description: \\\"Final price including taxes and add-ons\\\"\\n    - booking_id:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"Booking reference\\\"\\n```\\n\\nIn rules, you might then write:\\n\\n```yaml\\nwhen: conv[0].booking_id is not None\\nthen: extract_float(conv[0].total_price) > 0\\n```\\n\\nHere, `total_price` and `booking_id` come directly from `chatbot.output`.\\n\\n### 2.1.2 Designing `chatbot.output` with rules in mind\\n\\nWhen you design a profile, think about:\\n\\n- Which **business properties** or **behavioural invariants** you want to test with rules later (e.g., monotonicity of price, field completeness, uniqueness, topic scope).\\n- Which fields the rules will need to access.\\n\\nBest practices:\\n\\n- Use stable, descriptive names (e.g., `total_price`, `opening_hours`, `order_id`) instead of names tied to one particular experiment.\\n- Avoid duplicating the same concept under many different names across profiles; reuse names when semantics are the same.\\n- If you know you will write rules about a field, make sure it appears in `chatbot.output` and has the right `type` (e.g., `currency` instead of a raw `string`).\\n\\n### 2.1.3 Profile-bound vs global rules\\n\\nFrom the profile’s viewpoint, you will typically see two kinds of rules:\\n\\n1. **Profile-bound rules**\\n\\n   - Target a specific profile (e.g., `pizza_order_summary`).\\n   - Rely on its `chatbot.output` fields (e.g., `size`, `toppings`, `price`).\\n   - The rule should be updated if you rename or remove these fields.\\n\\n2. **Global rules**\\n\\n   - Apply to many profiles or the whole dataset.\\n   - Use generic helpers such as `only_talks_about`, `language`, `responds_in_same_language`, `repeated_answers`, `data_collected`, etc.\\n   - Do not require a particular `chatbot.output` schema to make sense.\\n\\nWhen you create or change a profile, ask:\\n\\n- “Which profile-bound rules might be affected if I rename/remove this field?”\\n- “Do I need to add a new field so that rules can express the checks I care about?”\\n\\nKeeping this contract in mind will make your rules and profiles evolve together without surprises.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3) Profile File: high‑level anatomy\\n\\nA profile is a single YAML file (or a **folder** with multiple YAMLs for batch execution). These are the top-level sections you’ll use most:\\n\\n```yaml\\ntest_name: \\\"string\\\"\\n\\nllm:\\n  temperature: float\\n  model: \\\"provider-specific name\\\"\\n  model_prov: \\\"langchain provider key\\\"\\n  format:\\n    type: text | speech\\n    # config: path/to/speech_config.yml   # (only for type: speech)\\n\\nuser:\\n  language: English | Spanish | ...\\n  role: \\\"prompt describing the simulated user\\\"\\n  context:\\n    - personality: personalities/<file>.yml   # optional\\n    - \\\"freeform constraints, facts, preferences …\\\"\\n  goals:\\n    - \\\"freeform goal with {{variables}}\\\"\\n    - variable_name:\\n        function: default|random|forward|another|pairwise(...)\\n        type: string|int|float|<custom>\\n        data: ... # list, range, generator, or LLM-generated list\\n\\nchatbot:\\n  is_starter: true|false\\n  fallback: \\\"bot’s real fallback message\\\"\\n  output:\\n    - field_name:\\n        type: <primitive|list[primitive]|custom>\\n        description: \\\"what to extract at the end\\\"\\n\\nconversation:\\n  number: <int> | combinations | combinations(0.6) | combinations(0.6, pairwise)\\n  max_cost: <float $>      # optional: cap spend for the whole run\\n  goal_style:              # how/when a conversation ends\\n    steps: <int> | random steps: <max> | all_answered:\\n      export: true|false   # export the verification dataframe\\n      limit: <int>         # safety stop; default 30 if omitted\\n    max_cost: <float $>    # optional: per‑conversation cost cap\\n  interaction_style: # choose one or many from here\\n    - long phrases | change your mind | change language: [italian, portuguese, ...] | make spelling mistakes | single questions | all questions\\n    - random: [any of the above] # there can be some interaction styles fixed and then some random, check the docs of the interaction_style section\\n```\\n\\n> Tip: Each **goal** can be a plain string (with optional `{{variables}}`) or a mapping that **declares** that variable’s `type`, `data`, and fill-in `function`.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4) Writing `user.goals`: variables, data, and functions\\n\\n### 4.1 Variables in text\\n\\nWrite prompts like:\\n`- \\\"Order a {{size}} pizza with {{toppings}} and {{cans}} cans of {{drink}}\\\"`\\n\\nEach `{{variable}}` must be declared elsewhere in the `goals` list with **exactly the same name** (case‑sensitive).\\n\\n### 4.2 Types (default vs custom)\\n\\n**Default types:**\\n- `int`: data as an integer.\\n- `float`: data as a float.\\n- `string`: data as text.\\n\\n**Custom types:** define a YAML file in `types/` that gives:\\n\\n- a `name` (must match the file name without extension),\\n- a `type_description` (prompt that explains the type),\\n- a `format` (Python regex for matching),\\n- an `extraction` schema describing how to parse the match into one or more typed values.\\n\\n\\n> No `list` type is used in `user.goals `.\\n\\n\\n**Examples**\\n\\n`types/phone_number.yml`:\\n\\n```yaml\\nname: phone_number\\ntype_description: A phone number\\nformat: r\\\"^\\\\d{3}-\\\\d{7}$\\\"\\nextraction: str\\n```\\n\\n`types/currency.yml`:\\n\\n```yaml\\nname: currency\\ntype_description: A float number with a currency\\nformat: r'\\\\d+(?:[.,]\\\\d+)?\\\\s*(?:[\\\\$\\\\€\\\\£]|USD|EUR)'\\nextraction:\\n  value:\\n    type: float\\n    description: a float value\\n  currency:\\n    type: string\\n    description: a currency unit\\n```\\n\\n### 4.3 Data sources for variables\\n\\nYou can populate the `data` for a variable in several ways:\\n\\n- **Explicit list** (strings or numbers).\\n- **Numeric range** for `int`/`float` using `min`, `max`, `step` (or `linspace` for floats).\\n- **LLM-generated list** with `any(\\\"<instruction>\\\")`, optionally mixing with manual items.\\n  Example:\\n\\n  ```yaml\\n  data:\\n    - \\\"Fanta\\\"\\n    - any(3 soda drinks)\\n    - any(alcoholic drinks)\\n  ```\\n\\n- **Custom list function** (your own Python generator):\\n\\n  ```yaml\\n  data:\\n    file: list_functions/number_list.py\\n    function_name: shuffle_list      # or your custom function\\n    args: [1, 6, 2]    # can be completed with a yaml containing a list (args: list_functions/list_of_things.yml)\\n  ```\\n\\n### 4.4 Fill functions (how values are chosen each run)\\n\\n- `default()` → use **all** items.\\n- `random()` → pick **one** at random.\\n- `random(5)` → pick **N** random items (N ≤ list length).\\n- `random(rand)` → pick a **random count** of random items.\\n- `another()` → cycle randomly through options without repetition until exhausted.\\n- `another(5)` → pick N unique items each time; no repetition across conversations until options are used.\\n- `forward()` → iterate deterministically through items, enabling **nesting** to cover combinations (e.g., `forward(drink)` depends on `drink`).\\n- `pairwise()` → generate pairwise‑coverage combinations across **2+ variables** (greatly reduces total cases while still catching most 2‑way defects). A minimum of 2 pairwise assigned variables are needed to use it.\\n\\n> Nest `forward()` to produce a grid of combinations; use `pairwise()` on two‑plus variables to cover **every pair at least once** without full Cartesian explosion.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5) Conversation controls that matter for profiles\\n\\nAlthough not strictly part of “user definition,” these fields strongly affect how a profile will execute and end:\\n\\n### `conversation.number`\\n\\n- A fixed integer, or\\n- `combinations` → use the **largest** combinations matrix produced by `forward`/`pairwise`, or\\n- `combinations(p)` → use a fraction (e.g., `0.6` = 60%), optionally restricted to a function: `combinations(1, forward)`.\\n\\n> Important: a minimum of two nested forward or two pairwise functions are needed to be declared in the variables in the 'goals' field to define a \\n> conversation number from a combination matrix.\\n\\n### `goal_style`\\n\\nChoose one of:\\n\\n- Fixed `steps: N`.\\n- `random steps: M` (random 1..M, M ≤ 20).\\n- `all_answered:` with optional `export: true` and `limit: 20` (safety cap; default 30). When `export: true`, a .csv dataframe is generated containing which outputs have been satisfied.\\n\\nYou can also set `goal_style.max_cost` to cap **per‑conversation** spend; `conversation.max_cost` caps the **entire run**.\\n\\n### `interaction_style`\\n\\nThese styles alter how the user will talk, you can choose one or many.\\nInteraction styles are not natural language prompts, they are a set of reserved keywords that you can choose from, so never translate them or choose one that is not below.\\n\\n- `long phrases`: the user will use very long phrases to write any query.\\n- `change your mind`: the user will change their mind eventually. Useful in conversations when the user has to provide information, such as toppings on a pizza, an appointment date...\\n- `change language`: the user will change the language in the middle of a conversation. This should be defined as a list of languages inside the parameter, as shown in the example above.\\n  - Here make a list with the languages like: \\\"Spanish\\\", \\\"German\\\", etc.\\n- `make spelling mistakes`: the user will make typos and spelling mistakes during the conversation.\\n- `single questions`: the user makes only one query per interaction from \\\"goals\\\" field.\\n- `all questions`: the user asks everything inside the \\\"goals\\\" field in one interaction.\\n- `default`: the user simulator will carry out the conversation in a natural way.\\n\\nThere is also the possibility of using `\\\"random: [<interaction_styles>]\\\"`. This option allows creating a list inside with any of the interaction styles mentioned. Then, it selects a random amount of interaction styles to apply to the conversation.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n```yaml\\ninteraction_style:\\n- long phrases\\n- random:\\n    - make spelling mistakes\\n    - change language:\\n      - italian\\n      - portuguese\\n      - chinese\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 6) Chatbot output extraction (schema at the end of a run)\\n\\nDefine what you want extracted after the conversation, for validation or reporting **and for Sensei-check rules to inspect**. Each field you define here can later be read in rules as `conv[i].<field_name>`. Example:\\n\\n```yaml\\nchatbot:\\n  output:\\n    - price:\\n        type: currency\\n        description: \\\"final price for the order\\\"\\n    - time_to_ready:\\n        type: time(\\\"hh:mm:ss\\\")     # accepts natural-language format specifiers\\n        description: \\\"prep ETA\\\"\\n    - order_id:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"the order identifier\\\"\\n```\\n\\nDefault types accepted in `output` include the primitives (`int`, `float`, `string`) plus `time(...)`, `date(...)`, and lists like `list[int]` or `list[string]`. Custom types work here as well.\\n\\n- int: Outputs data as an integer.\\n- float: Outputs data as a float.\\n- string: Outputs data as text.\\n- time/time(\\\"format\\\"): Outputs data in a time format. An output format can be specified by adding a parenthesis with the desired format written in natural language. Ex: time(UTC), time(hh:mm:ss), time(show time in hours, minutes, and seconds).\\n- date/date(\\\"format\\\"): Outputs data in a date format. Following the same logic as \\\"time\\\" type, a date format can be specified in natural language. Ex: date(mm/dd/yyyy), date(day-month-year), date(show date in days, months, and years).\\n- list[type]: Outputs a list of the specified data inside the brackets.\\n\\n\\n\\n> Note that custom types can be used in both `user.goals` and `chatbot.output` because they are defined in YAML files with the following structure.\\n> \\n> Example:\\n> ```\\n> name: phone_number\\n> type_description: A phone number\\n> format: r\\\"^\\\\d{3}-\\\\d{7}$\\\"\\n> extraction: str\\n>```\\n>Only the `format` field is used in `user.goals`, whereas the `extraction` field is used in `chatbot.output`.\\n> \\n> This design allows custom types to be compatible with both fields. However, this does not imply that default types can be used interchangeably. For example, default types such as `list`, `time`, or `date` may be valid in `chatbot.output` but can raise an exception if used in `user.goals`.\\n\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 7) Full example profile (end‑to‑end)\\n\\nBelow is a **complete, runnable** profile that demonstrates variables, custom types, functions, and execution controls without copying the pizza example.\\n\\n```yaml\\ntest_name: \\\"rental_car_quote_smoke\\\"\\n\\nllm:\\n  temperature: 0.7\\n  model: gpt-4o\\n  model_prov: openai\\n  format:\\n    type: text\\n\\nuser:\\n  language: English\\n  role: >\\n    You are a customer trying to book a rental car for a weekend trip.\\n    Ask for availability, pricing, insurance options, and pickup/return details.\\n  context:\\n    - personality: personalities/calm-user.yml\\n    - \\\"You prefer automatic transmission.\\\"\\n    - \\\"You are a member of a loyalty program.\\\"\\n  goals:\\n    - \\\"Book a {{car_class}} car with {{transmission}} and {{seats}} seats\\\"\\n    - \\\"Pickup on {{pickup_date}} and return on {{return_date}}\\\"\\n    - \\\"Add-ons: {{add_ons}}\\\"\\n    - \\\"Ask for a total price in {{currency}}\\\"\\n    - car_class:\\n        function: forward()\\n        type: string\\n        data: [economy, compact, suv]\\n    - transmission:\\n        function: pairwise()\\n        type: string\\n        data: [automatic, manual]\\n    - seats:\\n        function: forward(car_class)\\n        type: int\\n        data:\\n          min: 2\\n          max: 7\\n          step: 1\\n    - pickup_date:\\n        function: another()\\n        type: string\\n        data:\\n          - any(3 dates within the next 30 days)\\n    - return_date:\\n        function: forward(pickup_date)\\n        type: string\\n        data:\\n          - any(3 dates)\\n    - add_ons:\\n        function: pairwise()\\n        type: string\\n        data: [GPS, infant seat, additional driver, insurance]\\n    - currency:\\n        function: random()\\n        type: string\\n        data: [USD, EUR, GBP]\\n\\nchatbot:\\n  is_starter: false\\n  fallback: \\\"Sorry, could you rephrase that?\\\"\\n  output:\\n    - total_price:\\n        type: currency\\n        description: \\\"Final price including taxes and add-ons\\\"\\n    - pickup_time:\\n        type: time(\\\"hh:mm\\\")\\n        description: \\\"Pickup time\\\"\\n    - booking_id:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"Confirmation / booking reference\\\"\\n\\nconversation:\\n  number: combinations(0.5, pairwise) # two pairwise functions have been declared\\n  goal_style:\\n    steps: 6\\n    max_cost: 0.1\\n  interaction_style:\\n    - random:\\n      - make spelling mistakes\\n      - single questions\\n      - long phrases\\n      - change language:\\n        - Spanish\\n        - German\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 8) Authoring workflow (minimal steps)\\n\\n1. **Initialize** a project (once):\\n\\n   ```bash\\n   python init_project.py --path /abs/path/to/project --name my-bot-tests\\n   ```\\n\\n2. **Create your profile** under `profiles/` (use the example as a template).\\n   If you need custom types, add them under `types/` (see §4.2).\\n   Optional: create `personalities/` YAMLs for reusable persona prompts.\\n\\n3. **Run Sensei** with CLI flags **or** via `run.yml`:\\n\\n   **CLI example**\\n\\n   ```bash\\n   python sensei_chat.py      --technology taskyto      --connector-params \\\"base_url=http://localhost,port=5000\\\"      --project-path /abs/path/to/project      --user-profile profiles/rental_car_quote_smoke.yml      --output /abs/path/to/output      --verbose\\n   ```\\n\\n   **run.yml example**\\n\\n   ```yaml\\n   project_folder: /abs/path/to/project\\n   user_profile: profiles/rental_car_quote_smoke.yml   # or a folder of profiles\\n   technology: taskyto\\n   connector_params:\\n     base_url: http://localhost\\n     port: 5000\\n   output: /abs/path/to/output\\n   execution_parameters:\\n     - verbose\\n   ```\\n\\n   Then run:\\n\\n   ```bash\\n   python sensei_chat.py --run-from-yaml /abs/path/to/project\\n   ```\\n\\n4. **Validate** your profile before or after a run:\\n\\n   ```bash\\n   python validation_check.py      --profile /abs/path/to/project/profiles/rental_car_quote_smoke.yml      --output  /abs/path/to/output      --combined-matrix      --verbose\\n   ```\\n\\nThis produces a JSON with any format errors and CSVs with the value‑combination matrices (great for inspecting `forward`/`pairwise` coverage).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 9) Best practices & pitfalls\\n\\n- **Keep variable names stable**—they must **exactly** match the `{{…}}` usage in goal strings.\\n- Variables declared in `user.goals` should be used in goal prompts.\\n- Prefer **`pairwise()`** to cover many options efficiently; use **nested `forward()`** when full grids are intentional.\\n- With `random(n)`, ensure **`n ≤ list length`**. With `another(n)`, you won’t get repeats until the pool is exhausted.\\n- If you test multilingual bots, try `interaction_style: change language: [...]` and set `user.language` to your default.\\n- For time/cost safety, set **`conversation.max_cost`** and/or **`goal_style.max_cost`**.\\n- Put **real bot fallback text** in `chatbot.fallback` to avoid endless loops.\\n- For ASR tests, switch `llm.format.type` to `speech` and point `config` to your speech settings.\\n- Keep custom `types/` regexes tight and accompany them with a clear `extraction` schema.\\n- Store commonly reused prompts as YAMLs under `personalities/` and reference them via `context`.\\n- When a range of values is needed, prefer using \\\"min max step\\\" (or linspace for float) listing rather than listing range separated values.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 10) Quick reference: functions\\n\\n| Function        | What it does                                                 |\\n|-----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|\\n| `default()`     | Use all `data` values.                                       |\\n| `random()`      | Pick one at random.                                          |\\n| `random(n)`     | Pick **n** random values (no more than list length).         |\\n| `random(rand)`  | Pick a random count of random values.                        |\\n| `another()`     | No repeats until options are exhausted.                      |\\n| `another(n)`    | Pick **n** unique values per conversation, cycling overall.  |\\n| `forward()`     | Deterministic iteration; supports **nesting by dependency**. |\\n| `pairwise()`    | Cover all pairwise combinations across 2+ variables.         |\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 11) FAQ\\n\\n**Q. Do I have to define `llm`?**\\nNo. If omitted, defaults are applied (e.g., model and temperature) and the format defaults to text. Add it when you need overrides or `speech` mode.\\n\\n**Q. Where do I put custom types?**\\nIn your project’s `types/` folder as separate YAMLs. Reference by name in `goals` or `chatbot.output`.\\n\\n**Q. Can I run a whole folder of profiles?**\\nYes—set `--user-profile` to a folder or put that folder path into `run.yml:user_profile`.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Ready-made template\\n\\nCopy this into `profiles/my_profile.yml` and edit:\\n\\n```yaml\\ntest_name: \\\"my_first_sensei_profile\\\"\\n\\nllm:\\n  temperature: 0.8\\n  model: gpt-4o\\n  model_prov: openai\\n  format:\\n    type: text\\n\\nuser:\\n  language: English\\n  role: \\\"Describe what the simulated user wants and how they behave.\\\"\\n  context:\\n    - \\\"Who the user is, constraints, preferences, availability, etc.\\\"\\n  goals:\\n    - \\\"Main request with a {{variable}}\\\"\\n    - variable:\\n        function: random()\\n        type: string\\n        data: [option1, option2, option3]\\n\\nchatbot:\\n  is_starter: false\\n  fallback: \\\"Paste your bot’s real fallback here\\\"\\n  output:\\n    - important_field:\\n        type: string\\n        description: \\\"What you want to extract/validate\\\"\\n\\nconversation:\\n  number: 2\\n  goal_style:\\n    steps: 5\\n  interaction_style:\\n    - random:\\n      - long phrases\\n      - make spelling mistakes\\n```\\n\\nHappy testing!\", \"doc_type\": \"profiles\"}]", "additional_kwargs": {}, "response_metadata": {}, "type": "tool", "name": "get_docs", "id": "0fef3a31-4320-4661-91d3-2d920776d597", "tool_call_id": "call_46xlS7migdhUzebVAqRoIHxL", "status": "success"}, {"content": "Great!
